concepts.name: Scope and Methodology of Economics
concepts.description: Economics is the study of choice under scarcity, divided into microeconomics (focusing on individual consumers, firms, and markets) and macroeconomics (focusing on aggregate national outcomes).

concepts.name: Scarcity and Opportunity Cost
concepts.description: Scarcity implies limited resources relative to unlimited wants, requiring choices that involve trade-offs. Opportunity cost is the value of the single best alternative forgone when making a decision.

concepts.name: Positive vs. Normative Economics
concepts.description: Positive economics deals with objective, testable factual statements, whereas normative economics involves value judgments about economic policy and societal choices.

concepts.name: Production Possibility Frontier (PPF)
concepts.description: A graphical model showing maximum output combinations of two goods using available resources and technology efficiently. The PPF illustrates productive efficiency, opportunity cost via its slope, and economic growth through shifts.

concepts.name: Theory of Demand
concepts.description: Demand represents the quantities of a good consumers are willing and able to buy at various prices. The law of demand establishes an inverse price-quantity relationship, creating a downward-sloping curve that shifts due to non-price determinants.

concepts.name: Theory of Supply
concepts.description: Supply describes the quantities producers are willing and able to sell at various prices. The law of supply states that quantity supplied varies directly with price, while changes in production factors cause the supply curve to shift.

concepts.name: Market Equilibrium and Price Dynamics
concepts.description: Market equilibrium occurs where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. Shocks shifting demand or supply curves alter equilibrium price and quantity, restoring balance from temporary shortages or surpluses.

concepts.name: Price Elasticity of Demand and Total Revenue
concepts.description: Measures the percentage change in quantity demanded relative to a percentage change in price. Its magnitude determines whether price adjustments increase or decrease total firm revenue.

concepts.name: Income and Cross-Price Elasticities of Demand
concepts.description: Income elasticity measures responsiveness to changes in income (identifying normal vs. inferior goods), while cross-price elasticity measures responsiveness to changes in related goods' prices (identifying substitutes vs. complements).

concepts.name: Consumer Choice and Utility Theory
concepts.description: Models how consumers maximize satisfaction subject to budget constraints, incorporating total utility, diminishing marginal utility, and indifference curve analysis to determine optimal consumption bundles.

concepts.name: Factors of Production and Productivity
concepts.description: Production utilizes land, labour, capital, and entrepreneurship. Productivity measures output per unit of input, driving firm production costs, factor returns, and standard of living growth.

concepts.name: Production Horizons and Cost Structures
concepts.description: Distinguishes between short-run production (with fixed inputs and diminishing marginal product) and long-run production (all inputs variable), establishing total, average, and marginal cost relationships.

concepts.name: Perfect Competition
concepts.description: An ideal market structure with many buyers and price-taking sellers of homogeneous products, easy entry and exit, and output determination where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, leading to zero long-run economic profit.

concepts.name: Monopoly
concepts.description: A market structure dominated by a single seller protected by barriers to entry. Monopolists set price and quantity by equating marginal revenue with marginal cost, resulting in potential efficiency losses.

concepts.name: Monopolistic Competition and Oligopoly
concepts.description: Imperfectly competitive market structures: monopolistic competition features many firms selling differentiated products, whereas oligopoly features a small number of mutually interdependent firms often analyzed using game theory.

concepts.name: Gross Domestic Product (GDP)
concepts.description: The monetary value of final goods and services produced within a nation over a time period, measured via spending, income, or production, with real GDP adjusting nominal values for inflation.

concepts.name: Circular Flow Model
concepts.description: A macro model illustrating exchanges of goods, services, factors of production, and money between households and firms, incorporating financial, government, and foreign leakages and injections.

concepts.name: Economic Growth
concepts.description: A long-run increase in an economy's capacity to produce goods and services, typically measured by growth in real GDP per capita and driven by technology, capital accumulation, and human capital.

concepts.name: Functions and Characteristics of Money
concepts.description: Money serves as a medium of exchange, unit of account, and store of value. Modern monetary systems rely on legal framework and public trust to facilitate economic transactions.

concepts.name: Commercial Banking and Credit Creation
concepts.description: Commercial banks act as financial intermediaries that accept deposits and create credit through lending, balancing returns against credit, liquidity, and systemic risks under regulatory frameworks.

concepts.name: Monetary Policy
concepts.description: Actions undertaken by a central bank or monetary authority to adjust policy interest rates, open-market operations, and liquidity to influence financial conditions, aggregate demand, borrowing costs, and macroeconomic outcomes.

concepts.name: Inflation
concepts.description: A sustained increase in the general price level of goods and services over time, measured via price indices, which reduces purchasing power and can be driven by demand-pull or cost-push pressures.

concepts.name: Unemployment
concepts.description: The condition of individuals who are without work, available for work, and actively seeking employment relative to the total labor force. Classified into frictional, structural, and cyclical types.

concepts.name: Phillips Curve Framework
concepts.description: A framework describing the short-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment, where stronger demand reduces unemployment while raising inflationary pressures, though long-run relationships depend on expectations and structural labor market factors.

concepts.name: Fiscal Policy
concepts.description: Government decisions regarding spending, taxation, and borrowing designed to influence macroeconomic activity, manage aggregate demand, and provide automatic stabilization during economic fluctuations.

concepts.name: Fiscal Multiplier
concepts.description: The measure of change in aggregate output resulting from a change in autonomous spending, influenced by marginal propensity to consume, leakages like saving and taxes, and economic conditions.

concepts.name: Public Debt and Sustainability
concepts.description: The accumulated stock of outstanding government borrowing used to finance investment, smooth taxation, or support downturns, assessed by comparing interest costs, growth rates, primary balance, and revenue capacity.

concepts.name: Comparative Advantage
concepts.description: An economic principle explaining mutually beneficial trade when a country can produce a good at a lower relative opportunity cost than another, regardless of absolute productivity levels.

concepts.name: Balance of Payments
concepts.description: A record of a country's economic transactions with the rest of the world, including current-account trade and income flows as well as financial and capital transfers.

concepts.name: Exchange Rates
concepts.description: The price of one currency in terms of another, determined by market forces or managed interventions, which affects import prices, export competitiveness, inflation, and trade flows.

concepts.name: Economic Development
concepts.description: A broad measure of economic well-being and structural change that encompasses living standards, health, education, choices, human capital, and institutions beyond simple GDP growth.

concepts.name: Income Inequality
concepts.description: The dispersion of income across individuals or households, distinct from poverty, measured by metrics such as the Gini coefficient and influenced by skills, returns to capital, access to education, and institutional factors.

concepts.name: Environmental Externalities and Sustainable Growth
concepts.description: Economic growth strategies aimed at enhancing well-being while addressing unpriced environmental costs and resource depletion through policy tools like corrective taxes, permits, and regulations.

concepts.name: Fundamental Economic Principles
concepts.description: Core foundation concepts in economics, including scarcity, opportunity cost, supply, demand, market equilibrium, price elasticity, and Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
